clinicalPearls: A distinct and clinically aggressive variant of corticotroph pituitary adenoma defined histologically by Crooke hyaline change
Crooke change is the accumulation of a ring of hyaline keratin filaments in the cytoplasm of corticotrophs, displacing secretory granules and the nucleus
In non-neoplastic corticotrophs Crooke change is a physiological response to high cortisol, whereas a Crooke cell adenoma is a tumour composed predominantly of such cells
It may be functioning and cause Cushing disease, or clinically silent and present with mass effect
It is recognised as a high-risk aggressive pituitary tumour subtype with a tendency to invade, recur and resist treatment
Tumours are often macroadenomas at diagnosis with cavernous sinus invasion
Diagnosis is histopathological, with immunostaining for ACTH and low-molecular-weight cytokeratin showing the perinuclear ring pattern
Close long-term surveillance is required because of the high recurrence rate
reference.pathophysiology: The Crooke cell adenoma is a corticotroph-lineage pituitary tumour in which the tumour cells display Crooke hyaline change, a dense perinuclear accumulation of cytokeratin intermediate filaments. In non-neoplastic corticotrophs this change is induced by glucocorticoid excess and reflects feedback; when it dominates a tumour it defines an aggressive adenoma subtype. These tumours arise from pro-opiomelanocortin-expressing corticotrophs and may oversecrete ACTH, producing Cushing disease, or be hormonally silent yet immunopositive for ACTH. The keratin accumulation is thought to accompany a more invasive, treatment-resistant biology, and the tumours frequently invade surrounding structures and recur after resection.
additionalDifferentials: Ordinary corticotroph adenoma causing Cushing disease without Crooke change
Other aggressive pituitary tumours and pituitary carcinoma
Sellar metastasis or other sellar mass
additionalInvestigations: Histopathology with haematoxylin and eosin showing perinuclear hyaline change
Immunohistochemistry for ACTH and low-molecular-weight cytokeratin demonstrating the perinuclear keratin ring
Proliferation markers such as Ki-67 and the mitotic count to gauge aggressiveness
Pituitary MRI to assess size and cavernous sinus or parasellar invasion
Biochemical assessment for ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism when the tumour is functioning
Visual field testing where there is chiasmal compression
redFlags: Radiological invasion of the cavernous sinus or rapid regrowth
Persistent or recurrent hypercortisolism after surgery
Rising proliferation indices suggesting aggressive behaviour or progression toward carcinoma
reference.prognosis: Crooke cell adenomas are aggressive, with high rates of recurrence and resistance to conventional therapy; multimodal treatment with surgery, radiotherapy and medical therapy is often required and long-term surveillance is essential, with a subset progressing despite treatment.
pitfalls: Grading it as an ordinary adenoma and under-estimating the recurrence risk
Missing the diagnosis without cytokeratin immunostaining
Assuming a silent tumour is a benign non-functioning adenoma rather than an aggressive corticotroph variant
Providing inadequate long-term follow-up after apparently complete resection
